title: Erysipelas and cellulitis: recognizing a skin infection and getting help
intro: Erysipelas and cellulitis are bacterial infections of the skin and underlying tissues. They can start through a crack or wound too small to notice and often affect a leg, although other areas can be involved. Cellulitis is different from cosmetic cellulite. Early assessment matters because an untreated infection may spread and cause serious illness.

sections.heading: Recognize changes without relying only on redness
paragraphs: Seek same-day medical advice for a new painful, hot and swollen area of skin, especially if it spreads or you feel unwell. Redness can be difficult to see on darker skin; warmth, tenderness, swelling and a change from the surrounding skin still matter. Erysipelas tends to have a more distinct edge, but appearance alone cannot reliably distinguish every infection. Mention fever, blisters, wounds, insect bites, recent surgery, diabetes, poor circulation, immune suppression or previous episodes. Other conditions, including a blood clot, may look similar and need different treatment.

sections.heading: Know which symptoms require emergency care
paragraphs: Call 112 for confusion, collapse, marked breathing difficulty or signs of severe deterioration. Rapidly spreading swelling, pain much greater than the visible skin changes, purple or black areas, or severe illness with fever can indicate a dangerous infection and need emergency assessment. Do not wait for every sign to appear. Infection around an eye is particularly urgent if there is eye pain, altered vision or difficulty moving the eye. Do not drive yourself if faint or seriously unwell. Explain the speed of change and bring your medicine list.

sections.heading: Take the prescribed antibiotic and agree a review plan
paragraphs: A clinician usually makes the diagnosis from symptoms and examination. Tests or wound samples may be needed in selected cases. Tablets may be suitable for a less severe infection, while severe illness can require hospital treatment and intravenous antibiotics. The choice depends on allergies, likely bacteria, the infected site and other medical conditions. Take the medicine exactly as prescribed; do not share it, use leftovers or stop early without advice. An abscess may need drainage by a clinician, not squeezing or puncturing at home. Ask how and when progress will be reassessed.

sections.heading: Support recovery and notice treatment failure
paragraphs: Rest and raise an affected limb when comfortable, while gently moving nearby joints as advised. Ask about suitable pain relief and wound care. A dated photograph or an outline marked by the clinician can help track spread, but should never delay help. Some skin changes settle slowly; worsening general illness or rapidly increasing pain needs urgent review at any time. Contact the treating service if there is no initial improvement within 2 to 3 days of starting antibiotics, or sooner if advised. New hives, throat swelling or breathing trouble after medicine requires emergency assessment.

sections.heading: Reduce the chance of another episode
paragraphs: Keep skin clean, moisturize dry intact skin and protect feet and hands from injury. Treat cracks between the toes, athlete’s foot and eczema with appropriate advice. If you have diabetes, reduced sensation or circulation problems, ask for a foot-care plan and check wounds early. Persistent swelling may need a longer-term management plan; discuss when compression is suitable rather than starting it on a painful infected limb yourself. Repeated episodes sometimes justify specialist advice or preventive antibiotics, but these are not needed by everyone. Clean and cover draining wounds and maintain hand hygiene.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: a small crack with a growing problem
examples.text: Milan notices a hot, swollen ankle after a crack develops between his toes. Because he also feels unwell, he seeks same-day assessment instead of treating the swelling only with cream. The clinician assesses the infection and the skin break.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: reviewing an antibiotic course
examples.text: After beginning prescribed tablets, Lira records the affected area and follows the agreed review plan. When the pain rises sharply and she becomes dizzy, she seeks urgent help rather than waiting for a routine appointment or taking extra tablets.
